structure.title: Episodes 1–3 · Stephen's morning
structure.text: A joke at breakfast, a history lesson and a walk on the beach take us further and further into Stephen's private language. The people with whom he shares a tower know just where to wound him. As his thoughts grow harder to follow, the hurt behind them remains audible.

structure.title: Episodes 4–12 · The morning starts again
structure.text: We return to breakfast in another house. Bloom buys a kidney, goes to a funeral and tries to place an advertisement. A newspaper office full of orators and a pub full of patriots each have their own ways of making this observant, sociable Dubliner feel like a visitor.

structure.title: Episodes 13–15 · Dublin after dark
structure.text: On a beach, in a maternity hospital and in the brothel district, other ways of telling take over. In the last of these episodes stage directions admit the dead, the absent and the impossible. An embarrassment Bloom could conceal in daylight can now acquire a voice and summon witnesses.

structure.title: Episodes 16–18 · Coming home
structure.text: The prospect of a hot drink and somewhere to sit brings two wanderers together. An extravagantly precise question-and-answer account inventories the house. Then Molly, about whom men have been talking all day, lies awake in it with a memory and vocabulary of her own.

people.name: Leopold Bloom
people.text: Bloom wonders how other people see a sign, smell a meal or feel inside their clothes. His trade pays him to guess what strangers want. With Molly, whom he loves and knows intimately, he can imagine several answers and shrink from asking the question.

people.name: Stephen Dedalus
people.text: Stephen brings theology, poetry and family grievances into the smallest exchanges. His intelligence attracts audiences. It also gives him elaborate ways of living with the last thing his dying mother asked of him.

people.name: Molly Bloom
people.text: Concerts, professional arrangements and the man arranging them matter to Molly in their own right. Her recollections can quietly overturn a scene that seemed perfectly intelligible when we had only her husband's side of it.

context.title: One city, one day
context.text: The calendar barely moves on 16 June 1904, but a smell or a tune can take someone back years. A funeral party, an advertisement and a man in an unfamiliar coat turn up along several routes. Dublin gradually becomes familiar enough for the reader to recognise a passer-by.

context.title: Homer in the street
context.text: The long journey home in the Odyssey gives Joyce an outline he can fit to a walk across town. An obstacle to getting home can be as ordinary as a lost key. Knowing Homer adds jokes and echoes. Following the errand at hand usually supplies a foothold.

notice.text: Listen for the fragments that keep coming back.
notice.why: A line of song can be a stray sound on first hearing. When it surfaces hours later, it carries the room, the singer or the thought someone has spent the afternoon avoiding.

notice.text: See who takes care of the body in front of them.
notice.why: Food for a cat, concern for a woman in labour and a cup of cocoa occupy space alongside speeches about art and nationhood. Bloom's most consequential thoughts often begin with somebody needing something quite small.

opening: Leopold Bloom goes out for breakfast knowing his wife expects another man that afternoon. He has errands to run, a funeral to attend, and hours to fill before going home. Joyce follows him through Dublin with an intimacy that respectable conversation could never permit: digestion, lust, grief, advertising jingles, kindness nobody notices. A day that would scarcely deserve a diary entry becomes an entire world, because almost everything that matters to the people living it happens beneath the level of news.
